(1) Article 6 ECH can effectively bar refoulement; (2) the ECtHR requires the denial of justice to be flagrant; (3) the Greek courts did properly engage with the ECtHR case-law on Article 6 EHR; (4) stricto sensu (as opposed to wide) proportionality should guide the courts when assessing whether Article 6 ECR can block refoulement.
(a) The Greek courts did not engage in the relevant ECt HR jurisprudence, which is why they did not properly assess the case under Article 6. However, they did reach the right decision.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: what is the power of Article ECHR 6 to block refoulement, in light of its absolute character and the fact that it does not require a flagrant violation of the right to fair trial in the receiving state?

the question whether the ECtHR's case law concerning non refoulement under Article 6 ECH can be used by national courts in the context of extradition to block the return of an asylum seeker to the requesting state.
the power of the right to a fair trial to bar extradition and the conditions under which this power is exercised.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ECtHR case of the eight servicemen, as far as Article 6 is concerned, should be viewed as an instance of stricto sensu balancing, in which Article 6 is used to bar refoulemnt in a case in which the object of legal process in the requesting country is a right that has special moral weight, namely the right to life, as well as a right to a fair trial.

Article 6 ECHHR, as a reason precluding refoulemnt, should be applied only in cases of flagrant breaches of the right to fair trial and only when the object of legal overseas proceedings is a right of special moral weight.
, in the case at hand, the eight Turkish serviceman's Article 6 rights were so morally weighty that they outweighed the costs associated with non refoulement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the context of the present case, a fair trial was at stake and, as a result, the Greek courts were justified in refusing to extradite the eight Turkish serviceman.
Article 6, as a reason precluding non refoulement, is not a mere proxy for Article 3 or Article 2.

Article 6 ECRH can bar refoulement in the context of extradition proceedings, and that, when assessing the existence of a risk of flagrant denial of justice in a requesting state, a court must also examine the object or subject of proceedings overseas, i. e. what rights and interests are at stake and the importance thereof.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when it comes to non refoulement claims based on Article 6, a two-step process is required: first, a flagrant denial of justice must be identified, second, stricto sensu balancing must take place.
Article 6 ECRH can bar non refoulement in a way similar to Article 3 and Article 2.
, when it comes to the question of whether a denial of justice may trigger non refoulement, the ECt HR's approach to Article 6 is not as clear as one would expect.
